checklist.fact: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD) through its Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD), created after Governor Hochul's April 2022 announcement of $350 million for workforce development.

The need is that AI-related jobs often require specialized education and training out of reach for low-income individuals, creating a risk that AI progress will disproportionately benefit those already privileged and leave underrepresented communities behind.

AI Prep is an applied training program with two tracks: Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) for low-income matriculating undergraduates seeking paid internships, and Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment via accelerated training or bootcamp.
OSWD seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep for Track A and/or Track B.
Funding is up to $2M per track (up to $4M total) for an initial term of up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need, and availability of funds.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the contract period will not be considered, and indirect costs are not allowable.
Program objectives require serving a minimum of 250 participants (priority for those serving more than 400), with over 50% low-income participants.
Most graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.

Applicants may be non-profit or for-profit and must have experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.
Proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, uploaded to a designated Dropbox; late proposals will not be accepted.
The anticipated schedule is: winner announced November 14, 2025, and contract start January 1, 2026.
Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief), Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) and Schedule A (standard ESD contract terms) are referenced but not included in the RFP PDF.

component_records.title: Bid administration and submission control
component_records.description: A bid manager runs the proposal as a controlled project against the RFP calendar: all clarification questions are drafted, reviewed and emailed to the designated RFP mailbox citing page and section by August 29, 2025, and the complete two-part folder (Administrative and Technical subfolders, named to the RFP convention) is uploaded to the designated Dropbox before 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, with a documented internal freeze 48 hours ahead and a named backup uploader. A submission checklist is signed off item by item, and no late or alternative-channel submission is attempted. This component also owns the restricted-period contact log so that all procurement contact stays with the designated ESD contacts.

component_records.title: Program management office and ESD governance
component_records.description: A named lead organization (per the RFP's team-lead requirement) runs a program management office with a program director, monthly ESD status reporting, a risk and issue log, and a single point of contact for the State Project Manager. Staff are named in the proposal and any change of assigned staff is notified to ESD immediately, and no subcontracting occurs beyond what the proposal lists without prior written approval. The PMO also owns the monthly timeline from planning through first-cohort internship or job completion and the annual performance estimates against participants served, low-income completion and placement rate.

component_records.title: Compliance, insurance and MWBE/SDVOB administration
component_records.description: A compliance officer assembles and submits the full administrative package in the RFP's required order — Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, State Finance Law §§139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire (filed within one year of submission), Iran Divestment Act statement, EO-16 and EO-177 certifications, OCSD-1/OCSD-2/OCSD-4, NYS Businesses form, ST-220-CA and W-9 — and manages the restricted-period contact protocol. Post-award it runs the 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation programs, including good-faith-effort documentation, quarterly MWBE Compliance & Payment Reports, quarterly Workforce Utilization Reports with gross wages, and the monthly OCSD-6 SDVOB report, plus deficiency responses within seven business days and waiver requests within five. It also procures and maintains the required insurance tower (CGL $1M/$2M, Auto $1M, Sexual Abuse and Molestation $1M, statutory Workers' Comp/Employer's Liability and Disability) naming ESD as additional insured with waiver of subrogation, and files conflict-of-interest and ethics disclosures.

component_records.title: Outreach, recruitment and intake for low-income participants
component_records.description: A targeted recruitment engine built on partnerships with New York colleges and universities, community nonprofits and workforce centers, with a published low-income definition, an online application, and a scored evaluation and selection process. Needs assessments at intake identify each participant's barriers (childcare, transportation, device access, work hours) and route them to wrap-around supports. Track A recruitment targets matriculating undergraduates; Track B recruitment targets unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented New Yorkers with barriers to employment. Recruitment is sized to exceed the 250-participant floor and to keep low-income enrollment above 50%.

component_records.title: Industry-informed AI curriculum (Track A and Track B)
component_records.description: An employer-informed curriculum built with an industry advisory council of AI researchers and practitioners, delivered as online courses with real-world machine learning projects and defined technical and professional learning milestones. Track A is a comprehensive program for matriculating undergraduates, scheduled either in-academic-year or summer format to align with employer internship hiring cycles. Track B is an accelerated bootcamp-style program with an immersive schedule available part-time or full-time, covering in-demand technical and professional skills plus professional development and credentials where applicable. Curriculum is reviewed each cohort against employer feedback and refreshed on a published cadence.

component_records.title: Employer partnership and placement engine
component_records.description: Dedicated employer partnership managers cultivate and maintain relationships with leading New York tech employers, securing written commitments to paid internships (Track A) and full-time AI roles (Track B) and feeding employer input back into curriculum. The team runs an employer-facing pipeline: role scoping, candidate matching, interview preparation, placement tracking and post-placement retention check-ins. Placement support continues until the majority-placement outcome is met and is reported monthly by track.

component_records.title: Participant supports: stipends, mentors and coaches
component_records.description: Every participant receives a stipend at a proposed level disclosed in the budget, plus wrap-around supports: an industry-experienced mentor, a career coach (Track A) or success coach (Track B) with a defined caseload, and barrier remediation funded through OTPS lines such as transportation, childcare and equipment. Coaches track attendance, skill attainment and completion risk weekly, and escalate to the program director. Skill attainment is measured through milestone assessments and a completion dashboard.

component_records.title: Hosted program-management, data and reporting platform
component_records.description: A hosted case-management and learning platform configured for AI Prep: applicant and enrollee records, low-income status, attendance and completion, internship and job placements, participating colleges and employer partners, and stipend disbursement tracking. It produces the monthly ESD report and the annual performance metrics (participants served, low-income completion percentage, placement rate) from a single source of truth, and supports the quarterly Workforce Utilization and MWBE/SDVOB compliance extracts. Security controls are configured to the ESD IT Security Standard Brief once obtained.

component_records.title: Budget, pricing and cost documentation
component_records.description: A line-by-line price proposal within the $2M per track / $4M both-track cap, with Personnel Services detail (job title, name, hourly or annual rate, fringe rate, percent time, cost to contract) and separate OTPS lines for stipends, wrap-around services, curriculum development, marketing and events, mapped month-by-month to the 18-month term. No indirect costs are included; any cost match is shown on the budget template as a scoring enhancement. The budget is built so each track can be priced and awarded independently.

component_records.title: Organizational qualifications and dual-track capacity
component_records.description: The proposal documents the lead entity's non-profit or for-profit status, its track record in workforce development in AI or similar fields, and experience across at least three of the four required domains (academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training, serving low-income populations, New York market work). Where both tracks are bid, a dedicated capacity and staffing plan shows how two programs run simultaneously with separate cohort calendars, shared services and no resource contention. Key personnel one-page resumes and employer commitment letters are included.

component_records.title: Training delivery, coaching and continuous improvement
component_records.description: Cohort operations run to a published calendar: onboarding, instruction, project work, professional development, placement sprint and alumni follow-up, with cohort size and training duration proposed per track. A continuous improvement loop uses completion, skill-attainment and placement data plus employer feedback to revise curriculum and coaching between cohorts, and produces the annual performance estimates ESD requires, justified by historical results and partner commitments.

items.text: The issuing body is Empire State Development (ESD), New York State's economic development corporation, whose mission is to promote a growing state economy, encourage business investment and job creation, and support diverse local economies through loans, grants, tax credits, real estate development and marketing.

The program is run by ESD's Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD), created under Governor Hochul's April 2022 $350 million workforce development investment to align training with employer needs and create opportunities for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented workers.

ESD frames the business driver as a risk that rapid AI advancement widens economic inequality, because many well-paying AI jobs require specialized education and technical training that lower-income New Yorkers cannot access.
ESD also points to tech recruiting practices that favor students at elite schools and those with personal connections to prominent technology companies, which AI Prep is meant to counter.
New York State is positioned as a key AI hub, with institutions such as Cornell Tech and state-backed initiatives such as Empire AI supporting advances in medicine, infrastructure and cybersecurity.
ESD currently has no administrator in place for AI Prep; it is procuring up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and run the program.

ESD wants up to two program administrators to design and deliver AI Prep, an applied AI training program that connects low-income New Yorkers to AI internships or jobs at leading New York tech companies.

Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) requires a comprehensive AI training program for low-income matriculating undergraduates that includes paid internship placements, industry-informed curriculum, participant stipends, mentors and career coaches, and employer partnerships.

Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) requires an accelerated training or bootcamp alternative to degree programs that gives low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment in-demand technical and professional skills, success coaches, stipends, credentials where applicable, and full-time AI job placement support.
The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for applicants proposing to serve more than 400, and over 50% of participants must be low-income.
The majority of graduates must secure paid internships or full-time employment in artificial intelligence or a closely related field.
The contract term is up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds, and the anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026.

Awarded administrators must track and report data including applicant and enrollee counts and low-income percentages, completion rates, paid internship and full-time placement rates, and participating colleges and employer partners, with the exact list set during contract negotiation.
Proposals are scored out of a maximum of 100 points by an ESD selection committee, allocated as Firm Qualifications 15, Experience 25, Project Plan 30, Cost of Services 20 and Diversity Practices 10.

The Project Plan must include a monthly timeline from planning through first-cohort internship or job completion, plus proposed training duration, cohort size, stipend level, and 1-page resumes of key personnel and employer partner letters committing to paid internships or full-time jobs.

Proposers must estimate annual performance against three metrics — total participants served, percentage of low-income participants completing the curriculum, and paid internship or full-time job placement rate — justified by historical experience or partner commitments.

The Cost of Services submission must be a line-by-line price proposal with PS detail (job title, name, hourly or annual rate, fringe rate, percent time, cost to contract) and separate OTPS lines including participant stipends and wrap-around services.
Questions are due August 29, 2025, ESD responds by September 12, 2025, and proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025; late proposals will not be accepted.
Interviews, if necessary, are scheduled for the first week of November 2025 and the successful respondent is to be announced November 14, 2025.
ESD reserves the right to conduct reference checks at its sole discretion and to use reference information in evaluating proposals.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period will not be considered, and ESD will invest up to $2M per track (up to $4M total).
Indirect costs are not an allowable cost under this grant, and there is no cost-match requirement although cost-matching earns additional scoring points.

Applicants must be non-profit or for-profit entities with experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.

Proposals must be uploaded as a two-part folder structure (Administrative and Technical subfolders) to the Dropbox link https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep; fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted.

The Administrative Proposal must include the Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, State Finance Law §§139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire, Iran Divestment Act Statement, EO-16 and EO-177 certifications, OCSD-1/OCSD-2/OCSD-4 diversity forms, NYS Businesses form, ST-220-CA and W-9, and failure to submit any may result in rejection.

The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, with Utilization Plans (Form OCSD-4) required at proposal stage and quarterly MWBE and monthly SDVOB compliance reporting thereafter.

The selected respondent must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, Commercial Auto of $1M, Sexual Abuse and Molestation insurance of $1M, statutory Workers' Comp/Employer's Liability and Disability coverage, naming ESD as additional insured with a waiver of subrogation.

Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief) and Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) are referenced but their content is not included in the RFP text, so bidders must obtain them separately.
Questions are due August 29, 2025 and proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, with late proposals not accepted.
ESD has no administrator in place for AI Prep and is procuring up to two program administrators, so the program office is stood up from scratch rather than transitioned from an incumbent.
The anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026, which sets the mobilization clock.
The contract carries a 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation goal with quarterly and monthly compliance reporting thereafter.
ESD points to tech recruiting practices that favor elite-school students and personal connections as the problem AI Prep is meant to counter, so recruitment must reach beyond existing networks.
New York State hosts AI institutions and initiatives such as Cornell Tech and Empire AI, which the curriculum advisory council can draw on for researcher and practitioner input.
Employer partner letters committing to paid internships or full-time jobs are a required part of the Project Plan, so commitments must be secured before proposal submission.
Participant stipends and wrap-around services must appear as separate OTPS lines in the Cost of Services submission.
The exact reporting data list is set during contract negotiation, so the platform's reporting schema must be configurable rather than fixed.
Indirect costs are not an allowable cost under this grant and there is no cost-match requirement, though cost-matching earns additional scoring points.
Applicants must have experience in at least three of four domains, so the lead entity's domain coverage is a qualification gate rather than a differentiator.

The 250-participant minimum and the 400-participant priority threshold are assumed to apply per track over the full 18-month term, so each track is staffed and priced to serve at least 250 participants across its cohorts.

The majority-placement outcome is assumed to be measured at first-cohort completion and at contract end, with a paid internship counting as a qualifying placement for Track A and full-time AI employment required for Track B.
The $2M per track cap is assumed to be inclusive of participant stipends and wrap-around supports, so stipend levels are set inside the cap rather than funded separately.
The program is assumed to adopt Pell Grant eligibility plus a documented income threshold as its low-income definition, subject to ESD approval at contract negotiation.

The ESD IT Security Standard Brief (Appendix A) is assumed to impose standard State controls — encryption in transit and at rest, role-based access, audit logging and incident notification — which the hosted platform will be configured to meet once the brief is obtained.

The Diversity Practices Questionnaire (Appendix B) is assumed to be a narrative and data questionnaire scored on documented practices, so the response is drafted from existing diversity, hiring and subcontracting records and finalized when the form is obtained.

Schedule A is assumed to be ESD's standard professional-services contract with no unusual terms, so objections are limited to insurance limits, data ownership and termination provisions and are filed with the Administrative Proposal.
The budget template is assumed to require cost match to be shown as a separate column against each line, so the budget is built with a match column that can be zero-filled if no match is offered.

Participant floor and priority threshold undefined per track. The RFP sets a 250-participant minimum and priority above 400 but does not say whether that is per track, per contract or across both tracks, nor over what period. The proposed solution assumes the floor applies per track over the full 18-month term and staffs and prices each track to at least 250 participants; if ESD meant 250 in total, the bid is priced far above what is needed and loses on Cost of Services, and if ESD meant 400+ per track, the staffing and stipend budget is understated. The count drives staffing, stipends and the $2M-per-track budget, and the RFP leaves it open; the solution resolves it by assumption rather than by a stated ESD position.

Stipends may sit outside the $2M per track cap. The RFP caps each track at $2M and both tracks at $4M but does not say whether participant stipends and wrap-around supports count against that cap. The solution assumes they do and sets stipend levels inside the cap, which means a low stipend that may weaken recruitment and completion; if stipends are in fact funded separately, the bid leaves money on the table and scores lower on Cost of Services. Stipends for 250+ participants per track are a large share of a $2M budget, so the answer changes the whole price structure; the RFP does not settle it.

Majority-placement metric undefined, creating acceptance risk. The RFP requires the majority of graduates to secure paid internships or full-time employment but does not define the measurement window or whether an internship alone satisfies the metric. The solution treats this as a contractual performance commitment reported monthly and assumes internships count for Track A and full-time AI employment for Track B; if ESD measures differently, the administrator can be found in default on an outcome it cannot fully control. Placement depends on employer hiring cycles and graduate choices, not only on program quality, and the RFP leaves the denominator and window open while the solution makes it a contractual commitment.

Employer commitment letters required before submission. The Project Plan must include letters from partner employers committing to paid internships or full-time jobs, and the solution relies on those commitments to justify its placement estimates. If the letters are thin or generic, the Project Plan and Experience scores drop and the placement commitment becomes unbacked; if they are strong, they still bind the bidder to employers who may not hire on schedule. The letters are a scored submission item and the basis for the placement estimate, and they must be secured before the October 1, 2025 deadline, which is a short window for employer sign-off.

Administrative forms and referenced schedules not in the RFP. A long list of mandatory administrative items — Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, State Finance Law §§139-j/139-k forms, Iran Divestment Act statement, EO-16 and EO-177 certifications, OCSD-1/2/4/5/6, NYS Businesses form, ST-220-CA, W-9, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire and Schedule B — are available only by link or not at all. Missing or misordered items can result in rejection of an otherwise strong proposal, and the Vend-Rep questionnaire must be filed within one year of submission. The RFP states failure to submit any administrative item may result in rejection, and the forms are not in the document, so completeness depends on external downloads the bid team must chase.

Appendix A IT Security Standard Brief not available. Appendix A, the ESD IT Security Standard Brief, is referenced but not included in the RFP, so the hosted platform's security controls are designed against an assumed set of standard State controls. If the brief imposes stricter requirements — data residency, State-hosted systems, specific certifications or audit rights — the platform configuration and possibly the hosting choice must change after award, at unplanned cost and delay. The document is missing from the RFP and the solution explicitly defers compliance until it is obtained, so the design is unvalidated against the actual standard.

Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire missing from a scored section. Appendix B, the Diversity Practices Questionnaire, is worth 10 of the 100 points but is not included in the RFP. The solution assumes it is a narrative and data questionnaire drafted from existing records; if it turns out to require specific certifications, MWBE/SDVOB status or data the bidder does not hold, the response is weaker than planned and up to a tenth of the score is at risk. The form is a mandatory submission item and a scored section, and it is absent from the RFP, so the bidder cannot know what evidence it must produce.

Schedule A contract terms unreviewed before objections close. Schedule A, the sample contract, is referenced by link and objections must be filed with the Administrative Proposal or they are waived. The solution assumes it is ESD's standard professional-services contract with no unusual terms and limits objections to insurance, data ownership and termination; if Schedule A contains, for example, broad indemnification, IP assignment over curriculum, or unilateral termination for convenience, the bidder accepts terms it cannot price or live with. The document is not in the RFP and the solution's assumption is untested; waiver on failure to object makes the downside permanent.

MWBE 30% and SDVOB 6% goals hard to meet in an AI training program. The contract carries a 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation goal with a Utilization Plan at proposal stage and quarterly and monthly compliance reporting thereafter. AI curriculum, platform and coaching suppliers are not obviously MWBE or SDVOB certified, so the bidder may have to document good-faith efforts or seek a waiver, and the recurring reporting adds administrative load the solution budgets only through one compliance officer. The goals are contractual and the reporting is recurring, while the solution's supplier mix is not yet shown to include certified firms; the RFP does not say how strictly the goals are enforced.

Insurance tower and additional-insured terms raise cost and timing. The selected respondent must carry CGL $1M/$2M, Commercial Auto $1M, Sexual Abuse and Molestation $1M, statutory Workers' Comp and Disability, with ESD as additional insured and waiver of subrogation. Sexual Abuse and Molestation coverage is not standard for a training provider and may be expensive or unavailable on the required terms, and the coverage must be in place at contract start on January 1, 2026. The requirement is explicit and the coverage is unusual for this type of provider; the solution lists the tower but does not show it is obtainable at the assumed price.

Mobilization to January 1, 2026 start is tight for a from-scratch program office. Award is announced November 14, 2025 and the contract is expected to start January 1, 2026, with the solution's own plan allowing months 0–2 for mobilization and compliance set-up. ESD has no incumbent administrator, so recruitment partnerships, employer commitments, platform configuration and staff hiring all start from zero in a holiday period; a slip pushes first-cohort placement past the 18-month term. The gap between award and start is about six weeks and the solution's phase plan already consumes two months before curriculum build-out, leaving little slack against an 18-month term.

Low-income definition and 50% target depend on ESD approval. The RFP requires the respondent to define low-income while referencing Pell eligibility, and over 50% of participants must be low-income. The solution assumes Pell eligibility plus a documented income threshold, subject to ESD approval at contract negotiation; if ESD rejects the definition or applies it strictly, recruitment must reach a narrower population and the 50% target and the 250-participant floor may conflict. The definition is a scored submission item and a performance target, and the RFP does not confirm that alternative definitions will be accepted.
